abstract: This paper investigates the characteristics of relational work in Participatory Design (PD) practices. Through three cases, we discuss how researchers encounter, engage with, and nurture relations during the early, often fragile stages of PD processes. Building on existing research of relationality in PD literature, we draw on empirical material to develop an approach for depicting and describing relational work. We situate our analysis within municipal care contexts, aiming to identify and articulate different forms of relational work and reflexivity. We reflect on how relationships emerge, unfold, and evolve throughout these processes. Our contribution is twofold. Firstly, we present an approach to analyse PD projects through a relational lens, grounded in empirical cases. We propose an extension of relational language to understand relationality through various dimensions of relational work and reflexivity in dialogue with existing PD literature. Secondly, we explore how relational approaches can be advanced in a more practice-oriented way. We propose an explorative lens allowing researchers to expose and familiarise themselves with relational aspects present in PD processes.

title: Encountering, Engaging with and Nurturing Relations in PD Processes - An Explorative Approach to Relational Work and Reflexivity

abstract: This paper explores and unpacks aspects of relationality by examining design engagements in a Swedish municipal care setting. Our exploration of relational perspectives on homecare is grounded in home care workers’ (HCWs) use of a workday scheduling and planning app. This paper presents empirical data generated through interviews and participatory observations, and identifies three themes: Manifesting relationality, Affectionating relationality and Tensioning relationality. Based on our understanding of relationality as it is developed in social care and design research, we discuss how relationality develops in everyday care, by juxtaposing this with real-life accounts of relational care. Then, we deliberate on the perspectives of designing care technology in relational care practices, such as homecare work. This paper concludes by emphasising the need for a greater acknowledgement of relationality in the design of future care technologies and suggests possible directions for further exploration.

title: Exploring Relationality for Future Care Technology Design

abstract: Participatory Design (PD) stems from early workplace projects where new technology and its impact were explored together with workers. While there is a long history of applying PD in the care domain, there is a lack of knowledge of professional care actors’ perspectives and understandings of Participation. To address this, we have explored how municipal care professionals in Sweden understand, perceive and attribute value to participation and how participation unfolds in their organizations. The paper presents a qualitative analysis of six workshops where about 50 care workers and managers at each workshop (i.e. ~300 care professionals in total) have explored and discussed how they and their organizations understand and work with participation and participatory processes. Based on the analysis, this paper provides researchers with insights on how municipal care actors perceive participation, and how that can affect co-design initiatives in the care domain.
